podcast.title: MTV Parent Company (1981)
podcast.body: Warner Bros., as the parent company of MTV, played a crucial role in the channel's early success. They owned numerous record labels and instructed them to actively participate in the video bandwagon, ensuring MTV had a consistent supply of new promotional content. "The good news is that the parent company of MTV, Warner Bros, owned a lot of record labels, and these labels were instructed to get on the video bandwagon so that MTV would have a steady supply of new product."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Visual Music Division
podcast.body: A few individuals at Warner Bros. Records recognized the potential of visual music early on and formed a division specifically dedicated to this idea. This was a natural extension for them, given that the parent company owned a major movie studio. "A few people at Warner Bros. records also recognized the potential of visual music and formed a division dedicated to the idea."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 1

podcast.title: Elvis Costello's Debut
podcast.body: Elvis Costello released his album "Spike" as his new Warner Bros. album in the winter of 1989. This marked a significant label signing for Costello, leading to his first and only US Top 20 pop hit with the single "Veronica." "Released in the winter of 1989 as the lead single from Costello's new Warner Bros. album, Spike."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Extravagant Album Promotion (1990s)
podcast.body: In 1998, Warner Bros. Records demonstrated the lavish budgets available for promotion in the 1990s by hosting a global listening party for R.E.M.'s *Up* album in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The label flew in journalists and radio and music channel personnel from around the world to listen to the record, charging all associated costs back to the band. "When Warner Bros. was prepping the release of REM's up album in 1998, they held a listening party in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fine for Non-Compliance
podcast.body: The Beach Boys failed to meet the May 1973 deadline imposed by Warner Bros for the release of Smile. Consequently, they had to pay a $50,000 fine for not fulfilling this contractual obligation, further adding to the legend of the lost album. "No lograron cumplir con esta condición y tuvieron que apagar una multa de 50 mil dólares."

podcast.title: Seymour Stein's Executive Role
podcast.body: Seymour Stein, founder of Sire Records, eventually became a vice president at Warner Bros. Records. "He ended up as a vice president at Warner Bros. Records eventually."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Smile Release Clause
podcast.body: After signing with Warner Bros., The Beach Boys were bound by a contract clause that mandated them to publish Smile before May 1973. This condition highlighted the continued mystique and commercial interest in the unreleased album. "la banda afirmó con Warner Bros, quienes les impusieron una clau su lábara publicar Smiley antes de mayo de 1973."
